passages.t: Woe to those who make unjust laws
passages.happening:
The poem of judgment on Israel ends with a woe. ‘Woe to those who enact unjust statutes and issue oppressive decrees’ (verse 1), to rob the poor of fair treatment and withhold justice from the oppressed, ‘to make widows their prey and orphans their plunder’ (verse 2).

‘What will you do on the day of reckoning when devastation comes from afar? To whom will you flee for help? Where will you leave your wealth?’ (verse 3). Nothing will be left but to crouch among the captives or fall among the dead. ‘Despite all this, His anger is not turned away; His hand is still upraised’ (verse 4).
passages.hearers:
This woe is aimed at lawmakers and officials. They did not break the law to rob the poor. They wrote laws that did it. The first hearers would have known that injustice can be made legal, and that the people who suffer most are those with no one to defend them: widows, orphans, the poor.

The questions of verse 3 are sharp. On the day of reckoning, the wealth gathered by unjust decrees will not save anyone, and there will be nowhere to leave it. The refrain closes the poem that began in 9:8 and goes back to 5:25.
passages.later: The law had said, ‘You must not mistreat any widow or orphan. If you do mistreat them, and they cry out to Me in distress, I will surely hear their cry’ (Exodus 22:22-23).
passages.asks: The woe falls on people who made injustice legal. Ask whether any rule you keep or enforce makes the weak your prey. And ask where you will leave your wealth on the day of reckoning.

passages.t: Assyria, the rod of God's anger, and its boast
passages.happening:
‘Woe to Assyria, the rod of My anger; the staff in their hands is My wrath’ (verse 5). God sends Assyria against a godless nation to plunder it (verse 6). ‘But this is not his intention; this is not his plan. For it is in his heart to destroy and cut off many nations’ (verse 7).

Assyria boasts. Are not all its commanders kings? Calno, Carchemish, Hamath, Arpad, Samaria and Damascus have all fallen, so why not Jerusalem (verses 8-11)?

When the Lord has finished his work against Zion, he will punish the king of Assyria ‘for the fruit of his arrogant heart and the proud look in his eyes’ (verse 12). For the king says, by the strength of his hand and his own wisdom he has done this, gathering the wealth of nations like eggs from a nest (verses 13-14). ‘Does an axe raise itself above the one who swings it?’ (verse 15).

So the Lord will send wasting disease among Assyria's warriors. ‘And the Light of Israel will become a fire, and its Holy One a flame’ (verse 17), burning its forest until a child could count the trees (verses 16-19).
passages.hearers:
Assyria dominated the Near East in Isaiah's lifetime. Its kings, Tiglath-pileser III, Shalmaneser V, Sargon II (722 to 705 BC) and Sennacherib (705 to 681 BC), conquered and deported peoples from Mesopotamia to the borders of Egypt. The cities of verse 9 were all taken by Assyrian kings between about 740 and 717 BC. The boast Isaiah imagines mirrors the language of Assyrian royal inscriptions, which celebrate the king's strength and wisdom and list conquered cities one after another.

The chapter raises a hard question: if God uses Assyria to punish his people, is Assyria in the right? The answer is no. Assyria is a tool in God's hand. A tool that boasts against the hand that wields it will be broken. God intends just discipline. Assyria intends plunder, and takes the credit.

The first hearers, who had felt Assyria's power, were told two things at once: what they suffered was not outside God's purpose, and the power that made them suffer would answer for its pride and cruelty.
passages.later: Habakkuk says the same of Babylon later: God raises up the Chaldeans, yet ‘They are guilty; their own strength is their god’ (Habakkuk 1:11). And Joseph told his brothers, ‘what you intended against me for evil, God intended for good’ (Genesis 50:20).
passages.hard:
How can God use Assyria's cruelty as his instrument and then punish Assyria for it?

The chapter raises this directly. God sends Assyria against a godless nation (verse 6), yet Assyria's own intention is simply to destroy many nations (verse 7), and God will punish its arrogant heart (verse 12). The Bible's answer is that God's purpose and Assyria's purpose are different even when they work through the same events. Assyria is judged for what it intends and for its pride, not for serving God's purpose without knowing it. Theologians describe this as God's providence working through human causes without making him the author of their evil.

Some readers find this unsatisfying and ask why God would use cruel means at all. The chapter does not fully answer that. But it insists that God is not indifferent to the cruelty, that the instrument is held to account, and that the judgment serves a purpose that ends in a remnant's return.

This is a word about Assyria in Isaiah's day. It is not a key for saying that any nation's wars, or any people's suffering, are God's judgment now.
passages.asks: Assyria was a tool that thought it was the hand. Ask where you have taken credit for what God was doing through you. And ask whether you are confusing the success of the powerful with God's approval of them.

passages.t: A remnant will return, and Do not fear Assyria
passages.happening:
On that day the remnant of Israel will no longer lean on the one who struck them, ‘but they will truly rely on the LORD, the Holy One of Israel’ (verse 20). A remnant will return to the Mighty God (verse 21). Though Israel be like the sand of the sea, ‘only a remnant will return’ (verse 22). Destruction has been decreed, overflowing with righteousness (verses 22-23).

So the Lord says, ‘O My people who dwell in Zion, do not fear Assyria’ (verse 24), who strikes with a rod as Egypt did. ‘For in just a little while My fury against you will subside’ (verse 25). The LORD will strike Assyria as he struck Midian at the rock of Oreb, and raise his staff over the sea as in Egypt (verse 26). On that day the burden will be lifted from their shoulders and the yoke from their neck (verse 27).
passages.hearers:
Isaiah's son was named Shear-jashub, a remnant will return. Here the name becomes a promise. The remnant will not lean on Assyria, as Ahaz did. They will lean on God, whom 9:6 called the Mighty God.

The remnant is both a threat and a hope. Only a remnant will return, out of a people as many as the sand. But a remnant will return.

The second half of the passage reaches back to the exodus and to Gideon. As God struck Midian and parted the sea, he will lift the Assyrian yoke. The first hearers were told to remember what God had done before, and not to fear.
passages.later: Paul quotes verse 22 to speak of his own people: ‘Though the number of the Israelites is like the sand of the sea, only the remnant will be saved’ (Romans 9:27). Gideon's victory over Midian is told in Judges, where the LORD set the enemy ‘against one another with their swords’ (Judges 7:22).
passages.asks: The remnant would no longer depend on the one who struck them. Ask whether you lean on something that has hurt you because it seems strong. And ask what God has done before in your life that you need to remember now.

passages.t: The enemy marches, and the forest is felled
passages.happening:
The poem traces an army moving toward Jerusalem. ‘Assyria has entered Aiath and passed through Migron, storing their supplies at Michmash’ (verse 28). They cross at the ford and camp at Geba; Ramah trembles, and Gibeah of Saul flees (verse 29). Gallim, Laishah and Anathoth cry out; Madmenah and Gebim flee (verses 30-31). ‘Yet today they will halt at Nob, shaking a fist at the mount of Daughter Zion, at the hill of Jerusalem’ (verse 32).

Then: ‘Behold, the Lord GOD of Hosts will lop off the branches with terrifying power. The tall trees will be cut down, the lofty ones will be felled’ (verse 33). He will clear the thickets with an axe, ‘and Lebanon will fall before the Mighty One’ (verse 34).
passages.hearers:
The towns of verses 28 to 32 lie in the territory of Benjamin, just north of Jerusalem, and the march ends at Nob, within sight of the city. The first hearers could picture each step as the army came closer.

Scholars debate what event this describes: the approach of the Aramean and Israelite armies around 734 BC, an Assyrian movement, or a poetic picture of the threat rather than a record of a particular march. Sennacherib's actual invasion in 701 BC came mostly from the southwest, through Lachish. The book connects the sudden humbling of Assyria with the withdrawal of Sennacherib's army from Jerusalem in chapter 37.

The chapter ends with a forest being cut down. The next chapter begins with a shoot from a stump. God fells the proud tree of empire and raises up a small shoot from David's line.
passages.later: The next verse after this chapter answers it: ‘Then a shoot will spring up from the stump of Jesse’ (Isaiah 11:1). And Isaiah later tells of the night the LORD struck the Assyrian camp (Isaiah 37:36), as Kings also records (2 Kings 19:35).
passages.asks: The enemy came to within sight of the city and shook its fist, and stopped. Ask what threat in your life has come close and been stopped. And ask how the picture of a felled forest and a new shoot speaks to a loss you have seen.
